title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning
authors: Lianmin Chen, Junbin Qiu, Chenxing Wei, Yao Shu, Kun He
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliability in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results motivate the ZO-BOLT algorithm, which builds on BOLT's matched-data advantage for reliable ZO optimization of an RLVR-aligned objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.

infographic.key_insight: Zeroth-order gradient reliability hinges on data matching: mismatched evaluations amplify oracle noise as 1/μ², while matched evaluations cancel this amplification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: ZO-BOLT offers a route to RLVR-aligned LLM post-training with more reliable gradient estimates and a near-inference memory footprint.
method: Analyze matched versus mismatched finite-difference evaluations through a variance-theoretic framework.
Derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants separating the two regimes.
Build ZO-BOLT on Boltzmann Targeted SFT's matched-data advantage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched comparisons support the theory; experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over pretrained baselines.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports limited model and benchmark coverage; cancelling mismatch-induced amplification does not establish noise-free optimization.
infographic.paper_title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning

title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations
authors: Jiaxin Xie, Guowei Dou, Xiang Ji, Wensheng Yu
abstract: Mathematical formalization plays an important role in establishing rigorous and machine-verifiable foundations for mathematical reasoning. With the development of large language models (LLMs) and interactive theorem provers, intelligent agents offer a promising approach to automating the formalization of mathematical theories. This paper presents the Math Foundation Formalization Agent (MFF-Agent), a general-purpose intelligent agent designed to support formalization tasks across multiple mathematical domains. The agent integrates the reasoning capabilities of large language models with the formal verification capabilities of the Rocq proof assistant. It incorporates task classification, tool-assisted execution, verification feedback, and state-based task management to support the generation, refinement, and verification of formal proofs. Unlike an approach focused on a single mathematical theory, the agent is examined through case studies involving Morse--Kelley axiomatic set theory (MK), real numbers, propositional logic, and equivalences of the axiom of choice. These cases investigate its applicability across mathematical foundations and distinguish source-level completion, interactive verification, and reproducible compilation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of a unified operational framework for heterogeneous foundation-level tasks and clarify the gap between such a framework and a fully integrated mathematical foundation.

infographic.key_insight: MFF-Agent combines LLM reasoning with Rocq verification in a unified workflow for formalizing mathematical foundations across multiple domains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its tool-assisted, feedback-driven workflow offers a reusable architecture for developing machine-checkable proofs.
method: Classify formalization tasks and manage their execution state.
Use LLM reasoning and tools to generate and refine formal proofs.
Incorporate Rocq verification feedback into proof development.
infographic.evidence_signal: Case studies cover Morse–Kelley set theory, real numbers, propositional logic, and axiom-of-choice equivalences, distinguishing source-level completion, interactive verification, and reproducible compilation.
infographic.watch_item: A unified workflow is not yet a fully integrated mathematical foundation, and source-level completion should not be equated with reproducible compilation.
infographic.paper_title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations

title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning
authors: Yangrong Hu, Xueyu Zhou, Yue Wu, Jian Huang
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.

infographic.key_insight: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT) uses a frozen initial model with access to privileged information, such as ground-truth answers, to give greater training weight to tokens predictive of the correct outcome.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SPFT offers a token-weighted alternative to standard supervised fine-tuning for adapting language models to mathematical reasoning and code generation.
method: Analyze how dynamic and static token weighting change the target distribution.
Use a frozen initial model conditioned on privileged information to provide token-level weights.
Interpret the weighting through a Bayesian decomposition that favors outcome-predictive tokens.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements over standard SFT and other baselines across the main mathematical reasoning and code generation settings, without specifying benchmarks or effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Effectiveness depends on the quality of the privileged prior, and generating its token-level weights adds training-pipeline overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning

title: Embedding a de Rham Complex Structure into Eig-PIELM for Maxwell Eigenvalue Problems
authors: Hao Kang, Liang Li, Xing Li
abstract: The perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary condition alone does not eliminate the gradient nullspace of the Maxwell curl-curl operator. Consequently, a boundary-only Maxwell implementation of Eig-PIELM, an eigenvalue extension of the physics-informed extreme learning machine (PIELM), may retain represented gradient modes in its reduced trial space, producing nonphysical, gradient-contaminated modes. We develop dR-Eig-PIELM, a finite-dimensional structure-preserving extension that retains the linear-coefficient, boundary-null-space, and one-shot multimode architecture of Eig-PIELM. It combines compatible tensor-product grad--curl trial spaces with a constrained null-space construction to restrict the sampled PEC space to the mass-orthogonal complement of the represented gradient image before the eigensolve. Symmetric weak-form Gram assembly yields a symmetric-definite reduced eigenproblem without an eigenvalue cutoff under the stated sampling and material-positivity assumptions. For rectangles and cuboids, we establish fixed-degree exactness at the PEC vector-field space and derive rank and dimension identities. Numerical experiments show that dR-Eig-PIELM excludes the spurious eigenmodes with significant gradient components observed in the boundary-only baseline. The method exhibits rapid convergence with increasing polynomial degree and competitive work--precision performance in the tested configurations. A covariantly mapped waveguide example illustrates the potential of dR-Eig-PIELM for integration into design optimization workflows through a constrained local geometry update driven by computed cutoff frequencies and their sensitivities. This work provides a mathematical and computational framework for separating represented gradient modes from physical Maxwell eigenmodes within Eig-PIELM and supports its use in waveguide spectral analysis and geometry design.

infographic.key_insight: dR-Eig-PIELM removes represented gradient modes before the Maxwell eigensolve, preventing the gradient contamination that PEC boundary conditions alone cannot eliminate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports waveguide spectral analysis and geometry design using computed cutoff frequencies and sensitivities.
method: Build compatible tensor-product gradient–curl trial spaces.
Restrict the sampled PEC space to the mass-orthogonal complement of represented gradients.
Assemble symmetric weak-form Gram matrices for a one-shot, multimode reduced eigensolve.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper establishes fixed-degree exactness for rectangles and cuboids; numerical tests show exclusion of gradient-contaminated spurious modes, rapid degree convergence, and competitive work–precision performance.
infographic.watch_item: The symmetric-definite formulation depends on the stated sampling and material-positivity assumptions; the mapped-waveguide example illustrates potential rather than broad geometry validation.
infographic.paper_title: Embedding a de Rham Complex Structure into Eig-PIELM for Maxwell Eigenvalue Problems

title: What Drives the Zero-to-One Jump? Diagnosing and Steering Hard-Prompt Learning in RLVR
authors: Rui Zhu, Yumou Liu, Zhenzhe Zheng, Fan Wu
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved mathematical reasoning, yet progress on hard prompts often stalls: a prompt can remain unsolved for many training steps before abruptly transitioning to solved--a discrete "zero-to-one" jump whose underlying dynamics and steerability remain poorly understood. We investigate two questions: what drives this transition, and can it be steered? Through event-based analysis measuring the time-to-first-positive (TTFP), we find that negative rollouts preceding successful transitions consistently retain higher early-stage generation entropy, distinguishing near-solvable failures from dead ends. This signal motivates NAPO (Negative-Augmented Policy Optimization), a method integrated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that ranks negatives in unsolved groups via an early-branching driver and assigns graded advantages, injecting informative gradients precisely where standard group-relative updates vanish. Under fixed rollout budgets, NAPO accelerates early solution discovery and improves Pass@256 by 10.0 points on AIME24 and 6.6 points on AIME2025, demonstrating that zero-to-one transitions are diagnosable and steerable through driver-guided negative learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/jameszhu-pixel-time/Z2O.

infographic.key_insight: Hard math prompts can jump from unsolved to solved, and higher early-generation entropy in failed attempts helps identify failures worth learning from.
infographic.engineering_relevance: RLVR training can use informative failed rollouts to provide learning signals when standard group-relative updates vanish on entirely unsolved groups.
method: Analyze zero-to-one transitions using time-to-first-positive (TTFP).
Rank failed rollouts in unsolved groups with an early-branching driver.
Integrate NAPO with GRPO to assign graded advantages to those failures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under fixed rollout budgets, NAPO accelerated early solution discovery and improved Pass@256 by 10.0 points on AIME24 and 6.6 points on AIME2025.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports math-benchmark gains but does not establish whether the negative-ranking signal generalizes to other tasks or model scales.
infographic.paper_title: What Drives the Zero-to-One Jump? Diagnosing and Steering Hard-Prompt Learning in RLVR

title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
authors: Simon Matrenok, Nicolas Menet, Nicolas Flammarion, Andreas Krause
abstract: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.

infographic.key_insight: Repeated-sampling objectives reduce sharpening by shifting learning pressure toward harder prompts, and standard single-completion objectives can recover the same optimal policies with prompt-adaptive adjustments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: KAPPO adapts existing policy optimization methods to repeated-sampling objectives without changing their training procedures, enabling lower-cost control over behavioral coverage.
method: Derive closed-form optimal policies for KL-regularized pass@k and max@k objectives.
Recover those optima using prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation.
Apply KAPPO after a one-time reference calibration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments across several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation report sharpening control and single-completion training that matches multi-completion optimizers at a fraction of the cost.
infographic.watch_item: KAPPO requires reference calibration; the abstract does not quantify calibration overhead or sensitivity to its accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training

title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
authors: Zhenghao Li, Shengbo Wang, Nian Si
abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $cμ$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $μ$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

infographic.key_insight: Prioritizing requests by cμ—holding-cost weight times effective service rate—is fluid-optimal for LLM inference scheduling under finite KV-cache memory.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Memory-aware priorities can reduce inference latency by accounting jointly for compute speed, memory bandwidth, and KV-cache capacity.
method: Model stochastic arrivals, heterogeneous request lengths, prefill, and decode under a finite KV-cache budget.
Reduce fluid dynamics to a multiclass single-server queue and prove cμ optimality.
Construct a feasible finite-system policy and prove convergence of its scaled dynamics to the optimal fluid policy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on a real LLM serving engine with an NVIDIA H800 report substantially lower average latency while maintaining high throughput; the abstract gives no numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: Optimality is established in the fluid limit; finite-system benefits depend on practical implementation and workload characteristics.
infographic.paper_title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint

title: A Universal Policy Wrapper With Guarantees
authors: Georgiy Malaniya, Anton Bolychev, Pavel Osinenko
abstract: Many control tasks require driving the system into a prescribed goal set and subsequently keeping it there. The considered setting assumes that a working controller is available that provably reaches and maintains the goal, albeit with suboptimal performance. This controller is referred to as the fallback policy. Conversely, although state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning (RL) algorithms can discover policies with impressive empirical performance, the neural networks at their core act as opaque black boxes learned through data-driven exploration and, as such, provide no theoretical mechanism to guarantee that the system will ever reach---and stay within---the prescribed goal set. This article presents CALF-Wrapper, a method that combines the fallback policy with a pretrained RL base policy and uses the critic estimate associated with the base policy to select between them during deployment. The theoretical analysis establishes that CALF-Wrapper inherits the goal-reaching property of the fallback policy under the stated assumptions and provides probability bounds for the settling time and the maximum distance from the goal set over a prescribed time interval. The experimental study evaluates CALF-Wrapper in four simulated control environments of different complexity. Comparisons include the base policy, fallback policy, and constrained reinforcement-learning methods formulated for the same objective. Sensitivity and ablation studies provide direct hyperparameter recommendations. The experiments show how CALF-Wrapper can provide effective task performance while attaining the maximum possible observed goal-reaching rate. CALF-Wrapper requires no additional dynamics model, online learning, or constrained optimization during execution.

infographic.key_insight: CALF-Wrapper combines a pretrained RL policy with a proven fallback controller, inheriting the fallback’s goal-reaching and goal-maintenance guarantees under stated assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a way to deploy high-performing RL control with goal-reaching guarantees without additional dynamics models, online learning, or runtime constrained optimization.
method: Start with a pretrained RL base policy and a fallback controller that provably reaches and maintains the goal.
Use the base policy’s critic estimate to select between the two policies during deployment.
Establish goal-reaching guarantees and probability bounds on settling time and maximum distance from the goal.
infographic.evidence_signal: Four simulated control environments compare CALF-Wrapper with base, fallback, and constrained-RL policies; experiments report effective performance and the maximum possible observed goal-reaching rate, with sensitivity and ablation studies.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees depend on the stated assumptions and a valid fallback controller; simulation results do not establish real-world reliability.
infographic.paper_title: A Universal Policy Wrapper With Guarantees

title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition
authors: Andrea Violante, Nicola Rares Franco, Andrea Manzoni
abstract: Reduced-order models (ROMs) learned from trusted numerical simulations enable the real-time simulation of complex physical systems, making computationally prohibitive tasks-such as uncertainty quantification and optimal control-tractable. In particular, data-driven ROMs are opening the opportunity to learn from both numerical simulations and experimental data. However, integrating these sources of information is far from straightforward. Real-world measurements often involve multiple sources of uncertainty, including non-Gaussian noise, latent heterogeneities, unknown or hidden system parameters, and multiscale phenomena occurring below the resolution of the data. Consequently, real-world data are better described by parametrized stochastic partial differential equations, for which the development of effective ROMs remains relatively unexplored. In this work, we introduce POD-CNF, a data-driven generative ROM for efficient uncertainty quantification of parametrized high-dimensional systems. The approach combines projection-based model reduction and deep generative modeling. First, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to obtain a low-dimensional representation of the solution manifold. A Conditional Normalizing Flow (CNF) is then trained to approximate the density of the reduced coefficients conditionally on the input parameters. This formulation allows the surrogate to capture complex, multimodal output distributions, going beyond standard regression-based ROMs and least-squares predictions. We assess the effectiveness of POD-CNF through numerical experiments, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce output distributions while substantially reducing computational costs. Finally, a proof-of-concept application illustrates how the generative paradigm facilitates integration into Bayesian inverse problems, highlighting promising directions for future research.

infographic.key_insight: POD-CNF combines proper orthogonal decomposition with conditional normalizing flows to learn parameter-dependent solution distributions for stochastic PDEs, including multimodal outputs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate enables efficient uncertainty quantification for high-dimensional physical systems and offers a route toward Bayesian inverse modeling.
method: Compress solution snapshots into low-dimensional coefficients using proper orthogonal decomposition.
Train a conditional normalizing flow to model coefficient distributions given input parameters.
Sample reduced coefficients and reconstruct approximate solution fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate output-distribution reproduction with substantially reduced computational costs, alongside a proof-of-concept Bayesian inverse application.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify speedups or establish robustness outside the training parameter range.
infographic.paper_title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition

title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems
authors: Jiale Lao, Immanuel Trummer
abstract: For over 50 years, the database community has developed a wide range of successful engines to answer two fundamental questions: how can database systems run faster, and how can we ensure their correctness? Experience with these engines shows that performance depends on hardware and workloads. As both change over time, we repeatedly redesign and rebuild database systems, a time-consuming and expensive process. Correctness remains another long-standing challenge: recent studies continue to uncover wrong-answer bugs even in mature database engines, despite years of development and testing. To address these, we present GenDB-V, a system that enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized to hardware and workloads for performance, and formally verified for correctness. GenDB-V supports specialized implementations of SQL templates and general-purpose engines that accept any query within a supported SQL subset. First, we develop SQLSpec to formalize SQL semantics and deterministically construct fixed, implementation-agnostic synthesis targets. Second, we enable joint synthesis of fast code and formal proofs through storage--execution co-optimization, performance-first exploration, and three-layer modular proofs that bridge low-level execution to SQLSpec semantics. Third, we verify the synthesized code and proofs against the fixed synthesis targets in an isolated pipeline, proving SQL correctness and program safety. We evaluate GenDB-V on TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR. For verified template implementations, GenDB-V achieves geometric-mean speedups of 22.0-61.3x over DuckDB and Umbra. For a verified general-purpose engine, GenDB-V also achieves speedups of 1.27-3.4x on TPC-H. GenDB-V also achieves better performance than a testing-based LLM synthesis method, while our audit and tests expose incorrect answers in that method's implementations for 16 of 28 templates.

infographic.key_insight: GenDB-V uses AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized for speed while formally proving SQL correctness and program safety.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated, verified engine generation could reduce manual redesign as hardware and workloads change without relying solely on testing for correctness.
method: Formalize SQL with SQLSpec and construct fixed, implementation-independent synthesis targets.
Jointly synthesize code and modular proofs using storage–execution co-optimization and performance-first exploration.
Check code and proofs against the fixed targets in an isolated verification pipeline.
infographic.evidence_signal: On TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR, verified template implementations achieved 22.0–61.3× geometric-mean speedups over DuckDB and Umbra; a verified general-purpose engine achieved 1.27–3.4× speedups on TPC-H.
infographic.watch_item: Correctness guarantees are relative to SQLSpec and the supported SQL subset; the reported results do not establish coverage of full SQL or production workloads.
infographic.paper_title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems

title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes
authors: Andrew Gracyk
abstract: We attempt to alleviate failure modes of classical physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in scenarios of topological pathologies corresponding to punctures, holes, poles, and voids by introducing de Rham cohomological augmentations, or Hodge-de Rham PINNs. Vanilla PINNs often encounter pitfalls in hole-based settings due to discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed path integration, path dependence, correspondence to exact forms via the exterior derivative, etc., therefore we absolve traditional failures via parameterizing a 1-form by the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs (HMF) decomposition for manifolds with boundary, drawing a connection to de Rham cohomology such as through the HMF isomorphism theorem. 1-forms can act as representations of scalar-valued PDE solutions through integral operator mappings. We propose performing a PINN-based loss on the parameterized 1-form through an associated PDE, which subsequently solves the potential-based PINN problem and moreover remedies the failures of vanilla PINNs via the Sobolev-regular operator under a Fréchet differentiation interconnection. The operator relationship often has a nontrivial closed-form and often requires integration or a case-by-case analysis, which we address thoroughly in our experiments. When an integrability condition is not met on our losses, we can equip exhaustion functions to train the networks. We demonstrate our methods on the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which, to our understanding, is largely nonexistent in PINN literature. We develop theoretical guarantees of our methods and demonstrate our pathological safeguards on a broad selection of topologically-adverse problems, including scenarios of inexact forms, and those of nontrivial harmonics and coexact terms.

infographic.key_insight: Hodge–de Rham PINNs augment neural PDE solvers with differential-form structure to represent topology-induced behavior that conventional potential-based PINNs can miss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could improve physics-informed modeling on domains with holes, punctures, or voids where nonzero circulation and path dependence matter.
method: Parameterize a 1-form using the Hodge–Morrey–Friedrichs decomposition for manifolds with boundary.
Train with an associated PDE loss and connect the learned form to scalar solutions through integral operators.
Use exhaustion functions when the loss integrability condition is not met.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees and experiments on topologically adverse problems, including the Aharonov–Bohm effect, inexact forms, and nontrivial harmonic and coexact components, but gives no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The operator connecting form-based and potential-based problems may require nontrivial integration or case-specific analysis, complicating implementation.
infographic.paper_title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes

title: Some algebraic and geometric computations in CH via Chow forms
authors: Robert Andrews, Abhibhav Garg, Rafael Oliveira, Éric Schost
abstract: The problem of decomposing an algebraic variety into more structured components (such as equidimensional, irreducible, or connected components) is a fundamental problem in computer algebra and algebraic geometry. In this work, we study the computational complexity of computing equidimensional components of algebraic varieties, represented via Chow forms. We improve the state-of-the-art complexity bounds from PSPACE to CH, the counting hierarchy, for a number of problems related to equidimensional decomposition, including deciding (1) whether the Chow form of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety vanishes at a given point, (2) whether a given monomial is in the support of the Chow form of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety, (3) membership in a given equidimensional component of a given algebraic variety, and (4) membership in the closure of the image of an irreducible variety under a polynomial map. As an application of our algorithm to decide membership in the closure of the image of a variety under a polynomial map, we show that the approximate polynomial satisfiability problem can be decided in CH. We also show that the degree of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety can be computed in $\text{FP}^{\text{CH}}$. Our main technical result is the construction of a polylogtime-uniform family of constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits that compute the Chow forms of the equidimensional components of a given projective variety. We construct these circuits by combining the machinery of geometric resolutions together with the uniform constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits of Andrews, Garg, and Schost (FOCS 2026) for the multivariate resultant.

infographic.key_insight: Chow-form methods improve complexity bounds from PSPACE to the counting hierarchy (CH) for several algebraic-variety decomposition and membership problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results sharpen theoretical limits for symbolic-computation tasks involving polynomial systems, component membership, and polynomial-map image closures.
method: Represent equidimensional components using Chow forms and geometric resolutions.
Construct polylogtime-uniform, constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits using multivariate-resultant circuits.
Derive CH decision procedures and an FP^CH algorithm for component degrees.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical complexity guarantees, including approximate polynomial satisfiability in CH, rather than numerical experiments or runtime benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Exponential circuit size means the improved complexity classification does not itself establish a practical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Some algebraic and geometric computations in CH via Chow forms

title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry
authors: Bowen Li, Danqing Zhou, Chuan He
abstract: Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.

infographic.key_insight: A²ODA combines adaptive acceleration with low-cost p-norm preconditioning for unconstrained convex optimization, using a unified update structure for p ∈ [2, ∞].
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a line-search-free approach to large-scale first-order optimization without more elaborate updates for p > 2 than for the Euclidean case.
method: Use adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging with p-norm preconditioning.
Select step sizes through an aggregated affine lower model, without line search.
Analyze constant and gap-dependent curvature separately under generalized local smoothness.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence bounds, including a nearly optimal rate under local smoothness, but provides no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Practical speedups and preconditioning overhead remain unverified by the abstract; convergence guarantees depend on the stated smoothness conditions.
infographic.paper_title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry

title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction
authors: Faruk Alpay, Taylan Alpay
abstract: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosφ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.

infographic.key_insight: Nonreciprocal spherical attention yields a sharp coarsening-time exponent, while mass-centered compression gives quadratic attention-error bounds and skew score calibration admits optimization certificates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps engineers analyze compressed attention accuracy and calibrate approximate retrieval scores without assuming directional corrections outperform symmetric ones.
method: Prove the coarsening exponent 1 − cos φ for shrinking acute blocks under zero skew pairing and subexponential mass-ratio growth.
Bound fixed-temperature attention error by O(r²), including spherical-normalization correction.
Fit skew query-side corrections through a strictly convex moment problem with residual certificates and bounded low-rank projections.
infographic.evidence_signal: On SIFT1M, native-L2 hit@10 rose from 0.8926 to 0.8948 with skew calibration versus 0.8996 with symmetric calibration; a 10-million-vector index achieved 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms/query in a four-thread batch benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Skew calibration is not universally beneficial: validation selected no skew update for the 10-million-vector index.
infographic.paper_title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction

title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models
authors: Antonio Álvarez-López, Jingpu Cheng, Liyan Zhang, Qianxiao Li
abstract: Motivated by the expressive power of neural ordinary differential equations in flow-based generative modeling, we study the approximation of probability measures by pushforwards generated by parameterized families of Lipschitz vector fields. For Wasserstein distances, we establish a quantitative relationship between finite-sample point interpolation and distributional approximation, and derive universality criteria based on $L^p$-approximation of transport maps. In particular, affine-invariant families containing a non-affine vector field are universal from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures. For total variation, we show that coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient in dimensions $d\geq 2$ and establish sufficient conditions based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing. We further examine the role of point interpolation, establishing when different regimes relate to one another and when approximate interpolation can be made exact.

infographic.key_insight: Finite-sample point interpolation can quantitatively support distributional approximation by flow models, with distinct universality conditions for Wasserstein and total variation distances.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results offer theoretical guidance for choosing neural ODE vector-field families expressive enough to approximate target distributions.
method: Relate finite-sample point interpolation to Wasserstein approximation.
Derive universality criteria through L^p approximation of transport maps.
Use one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing to establish total variation sufficiency.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees, including Wasserstein universality for affine-invariant families containing a non-affine vector field from compactly supported, absolutely continuous base measures; no empirical evaluation is described.
infographic.watch_item: Coordinate-wise dynamics alone are insufficient for total variation universality in dimensions d ≥ 2.
infographic.paper_title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models

title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches
authors: Rileigh Bandy, Teresa Portone, Mohammad Khalil, Eric Crislip, Kyle Neal
abstract: Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.

infographic.key_insight: Staged closure learning trades moderately higher error for substantially fewer model evaluations and more robust optimization than embedded training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning closures offline from assimilated trajectories can reduce training costs for dynamical simulators with unresolved effects.
method: Compare embedded closure training with a staged data-assimilation approach.
Infer state and closure trajectories from observations, then train the staged closure offline.
Evaluate both approaches on a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear, state-dependent quarantine closure.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the synthetic SIQR evaluation, embedded training achieved the strongest average accuracy, while staged learning retained comparable qualitative behavior with moderately higher error and substantially fewer model evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from one synthetic exemplar; the accuracy–efficiency trade-off may differ for other systems or observation conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches

title: Nonparametric Intensity Estimation for Covariate-Driven Poisson Processes Using Deep Learning
authors: Atsutomo Yara, Yoshikazu Terada
abstract: We consider nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation of the intensity function of a Poisson process, allowing the intensity to depend on observed covariates. Such models describe how event rates vary with external conditions, including conditions under which the intensity becomes arbitrarily small or vanishes. However, risk analysis based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence typically requires the true intensity to be bounded away from zero, a restrictive assumption in applications. We develop a unified approach that avoids this assumption and derive an oracle inequality for the covariate-averaged Hellinger distance between the true intensity and the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE). As an application of the oracle inequality, we establish convergence rates for NPMLEs based on deep neural networks (DNNs). Our results show that, as in nonparametric regression, the ability of DNNs to capture underlying structure leads to improved convergence rates. Specifically, DNN-based NPMLEs mitigate the curse of dimensionality when the true intensity has a compositional structure and automatically adapt to a low-dimensional Riemannian manifold structure of the event space. For intensity functions with a compositional structure, DNN-based NPMLEs achieve nearly minimax-optimal convergence rates without explicitly incorporating this structure into the network architecture. Simulations demonstrate that DNN-based estimators outperform kernel estimators in most settings, while manifold kernels remain competitive in some designs. Finally, we analyze stimulus-evoked neural spiking using data from the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels project. DNN-based NPMLEs provide better out-of-sample performance than a conditional kernel estimator, as evaluated by held-out log-likelihood.

infographic.key_insight: Deep-network intensity estimators admit Hellinger-risk guarantees even when Poisson intensities vanish, with improved convergence rates under compositional or low-dimensional manifold structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports flexible event-rate modeling from covariates, including neural spiking applications where rates may approach zero.
method: Estimate covariate-dependent Poisson intensities by nonparametric maximum likelihood.
Derive a covariate-averaged Hellinger oracle inequality without requiring intensities bounded away from zero.
Apply the bound to deep networks, obtaining nearly minimax-optimal rates for compositional intensities and adaptation to manifold structure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations favor DNN estimators in most settings, and Allen Brain Observatory neural-spiking data show better held-out log-likelihood than a conditional kernel estimator.
infographic.watch_item: Performance gains are not universal: manifold kernels remain competitive in some simulation designs.
infographic.paper_title: Nonparametric Intensity Estimation for Covariate-Driven Poisson Processes Using Deep Learning

title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme
authors: Aboubaker Seddiq Benterki, Jüri Vain, Gert Kanter, Leelo Aino Jürgenstein
abstract: We introduce ALBI (Agent for Learning By Induction), a neuro-symbolic ILP framework that replaces the ASP-based hypothesis generator in the Learning from Failures (LFF) paradigm with a Large Language Model (LLM), while retaining SWI-Prolog as a formal verifier. ALBI implements an iterative generate-test-constrain loop: the LLM proposes candidate hypotheses from structured prompts; Prolog tests each candidate; and diagnostic feedback drives refinement. We further introduce semantic anonymization, a metamorphic testing methodology, to distinguish structural symbolic induction from surface-level pattern matching on predicate names. Experiments on 30 standard ILP benchmarks show that ALBI achieves 100% success across three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6), matching Popper while requiring only 1.4-1.7 iterations on average. Under anonymization, all models maintain 100% success with a moderate iteration increase (1.36-1.67 times), providing evidence of robust symbolic reasoning.

infographic.key_insight: ALBI pairs LLM-generated logic programs with formal Prolog verification to solve inductive logic programming tasks through iterative refinement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a generate-test-constrain pattern for combining flexible LLM proposals with executable symbolic checks.
method: Replace the LFF paradigm’s ASP-based hypothesis generator with an LLM guided by structured prompts.
Test candidate hypotheses in SWI-Prolog and use diagnostic feedback to refine them.
Anonymize predicate names to test robustness beyond surface-level semantic cues.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 30 standard ILP benchmarks, all three tested LLMs achieved 100% success, matching Popper with 1.4–1.7 iterations on average; anonymization preserved success while increasing iterations by 1.36–1.67×.
infographic.watch_item: Results on 30 benchmarks do not establish scalability to larger logic programs, and iteration counts alone do not capture runtime or LLM cost.
infographic.paper_title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme

title: Efficient Detailed Scheduling of Multiproduct Pipelines using Action-Decoupled Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Kai Shao, Ling Jian, Liming Liu, Serguey V. Bogomolov, Xinmin Wang
abstract: Multiproduct pipelines transport refined products to delivery stations in sequential batches, and their detailed scheduling must meet market demand while respecting nonlinear hydraulic constraints. Retaining the full hydraulic nonlinearity yields a mixed-integer nonlinear program that is computationally intractable, while the linearization commonly adopted for solver-based optimization degrades hydraulic accuracy without resolving the heavy computational burden. This paper develops an action-decoupled proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework that efficiently produces detailed schedules while preserving hydraulic fidelity. The scheduling process is cast as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) with flexible action durations. To handle the discrete-continuous hybrid action space, a cascaded dual-actor architecture decouples the discrete operating duration from the continuous flow decisions, eliminating the gradient interference that destabilizes conventional coupled-action policies and thereby yielding high-quality schedules far more efficiently. Validated on a real-world multiproduct pipeline in China and benchmarked against a single-actor baseline and a linearized MILP solved by Gurobi, the proposed framework achieves delivery accuracy close to the exact optimum while substantially improving flow rate stability and substantially reducing solution time.

infographic.key_insight: Decoupling operating-duration and flow-rate decisions enables PPO to generate efficient multiproduct pipeline schedules while retaining nonlinear hydraulic constraints.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports demand-driven pipeline operations with more stable flow rates and shorter scheduling times without relying on hydraulic linearization.
method: Model scheduling as a semi-Markov decision process with flexible action durations.
Use cascaded dual actors to separate discrete duration choices from continuous flow decisions.
Train with PPO to avoid gradient interference between the two action types.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a real-world pipeline in China, comparisons with a single-actor baseline and a Gurobi-solved linearized MILP report near-optimal delivery accuracy, improved flow stability, and reduced solution time.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify performance gains or establish generalization to other pipeline networks and demand conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Detailed Scheduling of Multiproduct Pipelines using Action-Decoupled Deep Reinforcement Learning

title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding
authors: Tom Szwagier, Xiaoyi Mai, José Henrique de Morais Goulart
abstract: We study a fundamental problem in machine learning: partial recovery of a planted signal $\boldsymbol{v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}$ from a spiked tensor $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{X}} = λ\, \boldsymbol{v}^{\otimes p} + \boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$, where $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ has symmetric Gaussian entries of variance $\asymp n^{-1}$. While previous works replace $\boldsymbol{\mathsf{Z}}$ by an i.i.d. standard Gaussian tensor to circumvent technical difficulties caused by dependencies, this paper directly analyzes the symmetric model via random matrix theory. We show that the square unfolding algorithm is subject to a sharp phase transition for partial recovery at $λ\asymp n^{(p-2) / 4}$, validating an open conjecture from Montanari and Richard (2014). We get precise expressions for the limiting spectral distribution, deterministic equivalent, phase transition threshold and overlap. The main message is that unfolded symmetric tensors spectrally behave like standard Wigner matrices, up to simple transformations accounting for high-order symmetries. We consider extensions to multiple orthogonal spikes, recursive unfolding and non-square unfolding via disproportionate random matrix theory, leading to an interesting conjectured statistical-computational tradeoff regarding the choice of unfolding: square versus long.

infographic.key_insight: Square unfolding of symmetric spiked tensors has a sharp partial-recovery transition at λ ≍ n^((p−2)/4), with spectral behavior resembling Wigner matrices after symmetry-dependent transformations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results clarify the signal-strength scaling needed for spectral recovery from symmetric tensor data without approximating dependent noise entries as independent.
method: Analyze symmetric Gaussian tensor noise directly using random matrix theory.
Derive limiting spectra, deterministic equivalents, recovery thresholds and signal overlaps.
Extend the analysis to orthogonal spikes, recursive unfolding and non-square unfolding.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical asymptotic results validating a 2014 conjecture by Montanari and Richard, but describes no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The recovery guarantees are asymptotic under symmetric Gaussian noise; the proposed square-versus-long unfolding tradeoff remains conjectural.
infographic.paper_title: A Random Matrix Analysis of Symmetric Tensor Unfolding
